page: Microsoft Azure E96ds_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8573C processor running at up to 4.2 GHz, configured with 48 physical cores and 96 dedicated vCPUs via multithreading. It features 260 MB of L3 cache alongside advanced hardware vector and matrix extensions, including AVX-512, AMX-Tile, and AMX-INT8. System memory totals 768.0 GB of RAM, establishing an 8.0 GB per-core allocation. Storage includes 5669 GB of integrated local NVMe SSD capacity, while no discrete GPUs are present.

Benchmark results demonstrate exceptional multi-threaded compute and data throughput capabilities. The CPU configuration achieves top-tier results in PassMark CPU tests, PassMark encryption, and extended vector instruction benchmarks, supplemented by strong Geekbench multi-core performance. Memory throughput is marked by high uncached sequential bandwidth, exceeding 506 GB/sec in large-block reads and 207 GB/sec in writes. Database and key-value performance tests highlight these hardware strengths, delivering over 122 million Redis SET operations per second and high-capacity database transaction results. In-memory LLM prompt processing achieves strong token throughput across small, medium, and large model architectures utilizing AMX acceleration.

The hardware composition exhibits distinct efficiency tradeoffs. With 8 GB of RAM per vCPU combined with high-capacity local NVMe storage, the server maximizes density for large memory footprints, reducing the need for sprawling multi-node clusters. However, single-core processing tasks register in the middle performance tier on stress-ng tests, indicating that workloads bound strictly to single-threaded execution do not extract maximum resource efficiency from this platform.

Microsoft Azure E96ds_v6 is engineered for large-scale enterprise databases, distributed in-memory caches, big data processing engines, and local NVMe-dependent analytics workloads. The inclusion of AMX and AVX-512 extensions also enables efficient execution of CPU-based machine learning inference pipelines that fit within system memory.
